tagline: A letter of hope from the apostle Peter to scattered believers in Asia Minor who were suffering as outsiders for the name of Christ.
overview:
First Peter is written to Christians who have become strangers in their own towns. Their neighbors find them odd, slander them, and sometimes abuse them, because they no longer join in the festivals, drinking, and religious life that once bound them to everyone else. Peter does not tell them that suffering is unreal or that it will soon go away. He tells them who they are: people born again into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus, chosen by God, a holy nation and a royal priesthood, heirs of an inheritance that cannot spoil. And he tells them how to live: with holiness, with love for one another, with honorable conduct that silences slander, and with the steady trust of those who follow a Savior who suffered before he was glorified.

The letter moves between the great truths of salvation and the ordinary settings where faith is tested: the relationship of citizens to rulers, household servants to masters, wives to unbelieving husbands, husbands to wives, elders to their flocks. Again and again it returns to one pattern, drawn from Christ himself, of suffering now and glory to follow.

First Peter has been loved by persecuted churches in every century because it takes suffering seriously without surrendering to despair. It gives readers a way to understand hostility that neither retaliates nor retreats, and it grounds that way in the cross and resurrection. It also contains one of the New Testament's most puzzling passages, Christ's proclamation to the spirits in prison (3:18-22), which has shaped Christian confession about Christ's descent to the dead.
author:
The letter opens with “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1) and closes with Peter calling himself a fellow elder and “a witness of Christ’s sufferings” (5:1). It says it was written “Through Silvanus” (5:12). Silvanus is almost certainly the Silas of Acts (the Greek and Latin forms of the same name), a leader in the Jerusalem church who later traveled with Paul (Acts 15:22, 40; 1 Thessalonians 1:1). The phrase may mean that Silvanus carried the letter to its readers, or that he served as Peter's secretary and helped shape its Greek, or both. Early Christian writers accepted the letter as Peter's: it appears to be echoed by Polycarp in the early second century, Eusebius reports that Papias used it, and by the late second century Irenaeus cited it by name. Eusebius counted it among the undisputed books.

Many modern scholars regard it as pseudonymous, written by a follower of Peter, perhaps a circle of his disciples in Rome, after his death. They point to its polished Greek and its use of the Greek Old Testament, which they think unlikely from a Galilean fisherman described in Acts 4:13 as unschooled; to its many parallels with Paul's letters; to the absence of personal memories of Jesus; and to what they read as a later situation of persecution. Those who hold to Petrine authorship reply that the help of Silvanus explains the Greek, that Peter had decades of ministry among Greek speakers, that shared early Christian teaching explains the parallels with Paul, and that the suffering described is local social hostility rather than an empire-wide campaign, which fits the 60s as well as any later date.
date: If Peter wrote the letter, it comes before his death, which early tradition places in Rome under the emperor Nero, most likely in the persecution that followed the great fire of AD 64. That points to about AD 62 to 64. The letter's calm counsel to honor the emperor (2:17) may suggest a time before Nero's violence against Christians became open policy, though Peter could have written it in the shadow of that violence. Scholars who regard the letter as pseudonymous usually date it between about AD 70 and 95, and some later, sometimes connecting it with conditions under Domitian or with the situation reflected in the letter of Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia and Pontus, who wrote to the emperor Trajan around AD 110 to 112 asking how to deal with people accused of being Christians.
setting:
The readers live in “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1), Roman provinces covering much of Asia Minor, the region of modern Turkey north and west of the Taurus mountains. The order of the names may trace the route of a messenger who landed on the Black Sea coast, circled through the interior, and returned near where he began, though that is a scholarly suggestion rather than something the letter says. These were mostly towns and countryside, not only the great cities, and the churches there are not described in Acts, except for parts of Asia and Galatia.

Peter calls his readers exiles and foreigners, borrowing Israel's language of the Dispersion, but most of them were Gentile converts: they had inherited an empty way of life from their ancestors (1:18) and had once lived in the pagan vices of their neighbors (4:3-4). Conversion cut them off from civic festivals, trade guild banquets, and household worship of the gods, and that withdrawal made them look antisocial and suspicious. The letter reflects slander, insult, and local mistreatment rather than an organized imperial persecution. Peter writes from “Babylon” (5:13), which most interpreters, ancient and modern, take as a code name for Rome, the imperial capital that like ancient Babylon ruled the world and held God's people in exile. Revelation uses the name the same way (Revelation 14:8; 17:5), as did some Jewish writings after the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. A few interpreters take it literally, as the Mesopotamian city with its Jewish community, or as a Roman fortress town called Babylon in Egypt, but these views have few defenders.
purpose: Peter writes, in his own summary, to encourage the readers and to testify “that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it” (5:12). He wants suffering believers to understand their identity (chosen, born again, God's own people), to see their suffering in light of Christ's suffering and coming glory, and to live in a way that commends the gospel to outsiders. The letter holds together two concerns that are often separated: faithful endurance under hostility, and respectful, good conduct within the structures of ordinary society. It aims to keep the readers from both despair and retaliation.
story: First Peter belongs to the period after the resurrection and Pentecost, when the gospel had spread well beyond Judea and communities of Gentile believers were learning to live as God's people without a homeland. It reaches back through the whole Old Testament story to describe them. Like Israel in Egypt, they have been redeemed by the blood of a spotless lamb (1:19). Like Israel at Sinai, they are called a royal priesthood and a holy nation (2:9, drawing on Exodus 19:6). Like Israel in Babylon, they are exiles waiting for home. Noah and the flood (3:20), Sarah (3:6), and the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 (2:22-25) all appear. The letter looks forward to the revelation of Jesus Christ at the end, the same hope the Bible's final book depicts.
christ: Christ is at the center of every movement in 1 Peter. He is the spotless lamb whose blood redeems (1:18-19), the living stone rejected by men but chosen by God and made the cornerstone (2:4-8), and the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 who “bore our sins in His body on the tree” (2:24). He is the example whose steps his people follow, who did not retaliate when he was abused (2:21-23). He “suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God” (3:18), was raised, and now sits at God's right hand with every power subject to him (3:22). He is the Shepherd and Overseer of souls (2:25) and the Chief Shepherd who will appear (5:4). Peter also sees him as the one the prophets searched for, their longing directed by the Spirit of Christ toward his sufferings and the glories to follow (1:10-11).
reading:
Read 1 Peter as a real letter to real people under pressure, full of the language of worship and early Christian teaching. Watch for its repeated pattern of suffering followed by glory, which applies first to Christ and then to those who belong to him. Notice how many Old Testament titles for Israel are given to a largely Gentile church, and ask what that meant for people who had lost their place in their own society.

The household instructions (2:13-3:7) need careful reading. They belong to a form found in ancient moral writing, the household code, which set out duties of wives, children, and slaves. Peter uses the form but addresses slaves and wives as moral agents with their own relationship to God, grounds their conduct in Christ rather than in the master's or husband's authority, and requires husbands to honor their wives as fellow heirs. Christians disagree about how these instructions apply today, especially regarding marriage; the letter itself nowhere endorses abuse, and its concern is faithful witness under unjust treatment, not the silencing of victims. Finally, 3:18-22 and 4:6 are among the hardest passages in the New Testament; the chapter notes set out the main readings.

structure.title: The identity of God's people
structure.summary: After the greeting, Peter praises God for new birth into a living hope, calls the readers to holiness as those redeemed by Christ's blood, and describes them as living stones built into a spiritual house, God's chosen people.

structure.title: Honorable conduct among outsiders
structure.summary: As foreigners and exiles, believers are to live so well that slander fails: submitting to rulers, servants to masters after Christ's example, wives and husbands in mutual honor, and all of them repaying evil with blessing.

structure.title: Suffering for doing good
structure.summary: Peter explains how to suffer for righteousness: with a ready defense of hope, after the pattern of Christ who suffered, died, and was raised. He calls for sober, loving community in the last days and for joy in sharing Christ's sufferings.

structure.title: Elders, humility, and final greetings
structure.summary: Peter exhorts the elders to shepherd willingly, calls all to humility and watchfulness against the devil, promises restoration after suffering, and sends greetings from Babylon.

themes.title: Living hope
themes.body: The letter opens with praise for new birth “into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1:3). Hope in 1 Peter is not wishful thinking but confident expectation grounded in a past event and fixed on a future one, the revelation of Christ. Believers are to set their hope fully on that coming grace, and to be ready to explain the hope within them to anyone who asks.

themes.title: Suffering and glory
themes.body: Peter never treats suffering as an accident or a sign that God has abandoned his people. He calls it a testing that refines faith like gold, a share in the sufferings of Christ, and a brief season before glory. He distinguishes suffering for doing good from suffering earned by wrongdoing, and he tells believers to entrust themselves to their faithful Creator.

themes.title: Exiles and God's people
themes.body: The readers are exiles, foreigners, and resident aliens, and yet they are also God's chosen people, a royal priesthood, and a holy nation. The loss of social belonging is answered by a deeper belonging. Their true home is the inheritance reserved in heaven, and their life on earth is a stay abroad lived in reverent fear.

themes.title: Good conduct as witness
themes.body: Peter repeatedly asks believers to do good, so that those who slander them may be put to shame and may even come to glorify God. This is not a strategy for avoiding trouble but a way of bearing witness under trouble, following Christ who entrusted himself to God rather than retaliating.

themes.title: Holiness
themes.body: Because the God who called them is holy, the readers are to be holy in all their conduct (1:15-16, quoting Leviticus). Holiness here means being set apart for God, which shows itself in turning from former passions, in sincere love for fellow believers, and in sobriety and self-control while waiting for the end.

keyChapters.why: Praise for new birth into a living hope, the call to holiness, and redemption by the precious blood of Christ.
The church as living stones and a royal priesthood, and Christ as the suffering servant whose example his people follow.
The call to be ready with a defense of hope, and the difficult passage on Christ's proclamation to the spirits in prison.
Joy in sharing Christ's sufferings, the only New Testament letter use of the name Christian, and the call to entrust oneself to a faithful Creator.

parts.body:
1 Peter is a letter of hope to believers who had become strangers in their own towns. It has five chapters and takes about twenty minutes to read aloud.

Its first readers lived in the provinces of what is now Turkey. Most of them had grown up worshipping the gods of their cities. When they turned to Christ, they stopped going to the festivals, the temple feasts and the drinking parties that held town life together. Their neighbours found them strange, and some insulted them, slandered them, and treated them badly (4:3-4). They had not lost their homes, but they had lost their place.

Peter does not tell them that their suffering is unreal, or that it will soon end. He tells them who they are. God has given them “new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1:3). They are God's chosen people, a royal priesthood and a holy nation, heirs of an inheritance that cannot spoil. And he tells them how to live: holy, loving one another deeply, doing good to the neighbours who slander them, and following a Saviour who suffered before he was glorified.

One pattern runs through the whole letter. It begins with Christ, and it is meant for his people: suffering now, and glory after. Peter writes as one who saw it: “a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and a partaker of the glory to be revealed” (5:1).

Some passages in 1 Peter are hard. It speaks to slaves and to wives in words that have been misused. It has one of the most puzzling passages in the New Testament, about Christ and ‘the spirits in prison’ (3:19). And it gives Israel's titles to a church of mostly Gentile believers. These notes set out the main readings fairly, take no side where faithful Christians differ, and name the misuses plainly.

The letter opens, “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1). Near the end the writer calls himself “a fellow elder, a witness of Christ’s sufferings” (5:1), and says he has written “Through Silvanus” (5:12). Silvanus is almost certainly the Silas of Acts, a leader of the Jerusalem church who later travelled with Paul (Acts 15:22, 40). ‘Through Silvanus’ may mean that Silvanus carried the letter, or that he helped Peter write it and shape its Greek, or both.

The early church received the letter as Peter's. It seems to be echoed by Polycarp early in the second century. Eusebius reports that Papias used it. By the late second century Irenaeus quoted it by name. And Eusebius counted it among the books no one disputed.

Many modern scholars hold instead that a follower of Peter wrote it after his death, perhaps a circle of his disciples in Rome, in his name. They point to its polished Greek and its use of the Greek Old Testament, which seem unlikely from a Galilean fisherman whom Acts calls ‘unschooled’ (Acts 4:13); to its many likenesses to Paul's letters; to how little it says of memories of Jesus; and to what they read as a later time of persecution.

Those who hold that Peter wrote it answer that Silvanus's help explains the Greek; that Peter had spent decades among Greek speakers; that the likenesses to Paul come from teaching all the early churches shared; and that the suffering the letter describes is local hostility, not an empire-wide campaign, which fits the 60s as well as any later time.

These notes do not choose. They call the writer ‘Peter’, as the letter does, and they receive it, with the whole church, as Scripture.

The letter closes, “The church in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you greetings, as does my son Mark” (5:13). Ancient Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC and carried God's people into exile. Most readers, ancient and modern, take ‘Babylon’ here as a name for Rome, the capital of the empire, where God's people again lived as exiles. Revelation uses the name the same way (Revelation 14:8). A few take it literally, as the old city in Mesopotamia or as a fortress town called Babylon in Egypt, but these views have few defenders.

Early tradition places Peter in Rome at the end of his life, and says he died there under the emperor Nero, most likely in the persecution that followed the great fire of AD 64. If Peter wrote the letter, it comes from about AD 62 to 64. Its calm call to ‘honor the king’ (2:17) may suggest a time before Nero's violence against Christians became open, though Peter could have written in its shadow.

Scholars who think it was written later in Peter's name usually date it between about AD 70 and 95, and some later. Some link it with the time when Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia and Pontus, wrote to the emperor Trajan around AD 110 to 112 asking how to deal with people accused of being Christians. These notes do not choose.

‘Mark’ is almost certainly John Mark, whose mother's house in Jerusalem was where Peter went when he was freed from prison (Acts 12:12). Peter calls him ‘my son’ in love. Papias, as Eusebius reports him, said Mark was Peter's interpreter and wrote down Peter's memories of Jesus.

The letter is sent to God's chosen “exiles of the Dispersion throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1). These were Roman provinces covering much of Asia Minor, north of the Taurus mountains: cities, towns and wide farmland. Paul had worked in parts of Galatia and Asia. No one knows how the gospel reached Pontus, Cappadocia and Bithynia. Visitors from Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia heard Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:9), and Acts says the Spirit kept Paul from entering Bithynia (Acts 16:7).

Some scholars suggest that the order of the names traces the route of a messenger who landed on the Black Sea coast, circled through the inland provinces, and came back near where he began. That is a suggestion; the letter does not say.

Peter calls the readers ‘exiles’ and ‘foreigners’, using Israel's words for God's scattered people. But most of them were Gentiles. They had been redeemed “from the empty way of life you inherited from your forefathers” (1:18), and they had once lived as their pagan neighbours did (4:3). Turning to Christ cut them off from the town festivals, the trade-guild banquets and the household gods. To their neighbours that looked antisocial, even disloyal.

So the suffering in this letter is mostly slander, insult and local mistreatment, not a planned campaign by the empire. It was still real, and it still hurt.

Who you are (1:1 to 2:10). Praise to God for new birth into a living hope. Trials that test faith like gold. The salvation the prophets searched for. A call to be holy, as people bought with Christ's blood, and to love one another. Then the living stone and the living stones: Christ, and his people built into a spiritual house, ‘a chosen people, a royal priesthood’.

How to live among neighbours (2:11 to 3:12). As foreigners, live so well that slander fails. Respect those who govern. Then a household code, a form of teaching common in the ancient world: words to household slaves, to wives, and to husbands. Then to everyone: do not repay evil with evil, but with blessing.

Suffering for doing good (3:13 to 4:19). Be ready to give a reason for your hope, gently. Christ suffered once for all, was made alive, proclaimed to the spirits in prison, and now reigns. So live for God's will, love deeply, use your gifts. Do not be surprised by the fiery trial, and do not be ashamed to suffer as a Christian.

Elders, humility, and farewell (chapter 5). Elders, shepherd God's flock willingly and as examples. Everyone, be humble, cast your anxiety on God, resist the devil. After a little while, the God of all grace will restore you. Greetings from Babylon.

parts.h: Suffering, and the glory to follow
parts.body:
Peter never treats suffering as an accident or a sign that God has left. He calls it a fire that tests faith “more precious than gold” (1:7), a share in Christ's own sufferings (4:13), and a short time before glory: “after you have suffered for a little while”, the God of all grace “will Himself restore you, secure you, strengthen you, and establish you” (5:10).

He makes a careful distinction. It is no credit to suffer for doing wrong. But to suffer for doing good, and to bear it without striking back, is to walk where Christ walked. “When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly” (2:23).

Some things these chapters do not say. They do not say that suffering is good in itself, or that God sends it as a punishment. They do not say that a person being harmed must stay and bear it if they can get away. The letter's words are spoken to people who often had no way out, and its answer is that God sees, judges justly, and will put things right.

Nor does Peter tell sufferers to carry it alone. The same letter calls the church to love deeply, to open their homes, and to pray. And it says, “Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you” (5:7).

If you are carrying something heavy now, these chapters do not ask you to pretend. Not every hardship comes from following Jesus, and not every hardship is meant to be endured in silence. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

parts.h: Chosen, and the people of God
parts.body:
Peter begins by calling his readers ‘the elect’, “chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father” (1:1-2). Christians agree that salvation begins with God's kindness, not ours. They understand his choosing in different ways. Reformed Christians read it as God's loving choice, before creation, of particular people for salvation, resting wholly on his free mercy. Arminian and Wesleyan Christians read it as God's choice of those he knew beforehand would trust him, with grace that enables but does not force. Others in both traditions stress that God chooses a people in Christ, as he once chose Israel, and that each person comes into that people by faith. These notes do not choose. All agree that God's choice is gracious and that it was given here to comfort people who had lost their place in the world.

Then, in 2:9-10, Peter gives his mostly Gentile readers the great titles God gave Israel at Sinai and through the prophets: “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession” (2:9). “Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God” (2:10), words taken from Hosea.

How does this fit with Israel's own place in God's purpose? Christians answer in different ways. Some hold that the church has taken Israel's place, often called replacement theology; others hold a milder view they call fulfilment, that God's promises to Israel are fulfilled in Christ and that Israel and the church are one people of God in him. Covenant theology stresses one people of God across both Testaments, and many who hold it also expect a future turning of Jewish people to Christ. Dispensational readings hold that God keeps a distinct future for the Jewish people beside the church. A few hold that Jews are in covenant with God through Moses and need not come to faith in Christ; most churches do not teach this. The notes on Romans 9 to 11 set out these views in their holders' terms. These notes do not choose.

On one thing this site takes a side. Peter is a Jew, writing in the words of Israel's own Scriptures, welcoming Gentiles into the blessings God first gave Israel. Paul, writing of his own people, asks, “did God reject His people? Certainly not!” (Romans 11:1). For centuries some Christians used the New Testament to justify contempt for Jews. That reading is false, and this site rejects it; the note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why.

In 2:13 to 3:7 Peter uses a form of teaching common in the ancient world, a household code, which set out the duties of each member of a household. But he changes it. He speaks to slaves and wives as people who answer to God for themselves. He grounds what he asks in Christ, not in the master's or husband's rights. And he tells husbands to honour their wives as “fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life” (3:7).

Rulers (2:13-17). Believers are to respect the emperor and his governors, whose task is to punish wrong and praise right. This is not approval of everything a ruler does. The same verse says, “fear God, honor the king”: fear is for God alone. When the authorities forbade the apostles to preach, Peter answered, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

Slaves (2:18-25). Peter does not command the end of slavery, and that should not be softened. He writes to a small, powerless movement in an empire where slavery was everywhere. But he speaks to slaves as members of the church and as people who answer to God, and he calls unjust treatment unjust. The history of verses like these is painful. In the Atlantic slave trade and in the American South, slaveholders and many preachers used them to demand obedience from enslaved Africans and to defend slavery as biblical, while they ignored the equality of all in Christ. That was a misuse, and it was wrong. The chapter note on 2:18-25 says more.

Wives and husbands (3:1-7). Peter speaks first to wives whose husbands did not believe, women in a dangerous place in a world that expected a wife to worship her husband's gods. Christians who share the same faith read his words for marriage today in different ways. Complementarians hold that men and women are equal in worth but given different callings in marriage, and that a wife's submission is a lasting pattern, freely given, never something a husband may demand. Egalitarians hold that men and women are equal in worth and in calling, that Peter applies the gospel inside the customs of his day for the sake of witness, and that the deeper principle is mutual submission and a shared inheritance. These notes do not choose.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. Abuse and other crimes are to be reported to the police and the proper authorities. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

parts.h: Christ, the spirits in prison, and baptism
parts.body:
In 3:18-22 Peter tells the whole path of Christ in a few lines: “For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God. He was put to death in the body but made alive in the Spirit” (3:18). Then come the hardest words in the letter: “in whom He also went and preached to the spirits in prison who disobeyed long ago when God waited patiently in the days of Noah” (3:19-20).

The church has read this in three main ways. Some, following Augustine, hold that Christ, by the Spirit, preached through Noah to the people of Noah's day, who refused to listen and are now held for judgment. Others hold that between his death and resurrection Christ went to the realm of the dead and proclaimed his message there: some early writers thought of an offer of salvation, others of freeing the faithful of old, others of a word of judgment. This reading stands behind the line of the Apostles' Creed, ‘he descended into hell’, whose older sense is ‘descended to the dead’. Many modern readers hold that the spirits are fallen angels held for their rebellion in Noah's day, and that the risen Christ, on his way to heaven, announced his victory over them. These notes do not choose. All three agree on Peter's point: Christ's suffering led to his triumph over every power, ‘with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him’ (3:22).

Peter goes on: “this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also—not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (3:21). All Christians agree that baptism's power comes from the risen Christ, not from the water. They differ on how baptism and salvation are joined. Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran Christians generally hold that God truly gives new life through baptism as his appointed means. Reformed and Presbyterian Christians often speak of baptism as a sign and seal joined to the reality. Baptists and many other evangelicals see it as the public sign of a salvation already received by faith. These notes do not choose.

And 4:6 says the gospel “was preached even to those who are now dead”. Many read this of believers who heard the gospel in life and have since died; others link it with 3:19. These notes say no more than the text does about anyone's place after death.

Peter writes in the language of Israel's Scriptures on almost every page. His readers are redeemed with the blood of “a lamb without blemish or spot” (1:19), like the Passover lamb. They are called to holiness in the words of Leviticus: “Be holy, because I am holy” (1:16). They are a royal priesthood and a holy nation, like Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19:6). They are exiles, like Israel in Babylon.

Christ is ‘the stone the builders rejected’ of Psalm 118, and the precious cornerstone laid in Zion of Isaiah 28. His suffering is told in the words of Isaiah 53: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth” (2:22); “By His stripes you are healed” (2:24). Peter quotes Psalm 34 at length (3:10-12), points to Noah and the flood (3:20), and holds up Sarah as a mother of believing women (3:6).

He also says that the prophets themselves searched to know the time their words pointed to, and that ‘the Spirit of Christ in them’ was speaking of Christ's sufferings ‘and the glories to follow’ (1:11). Peter often follows the old Greek translation of the Old Testament, so his wording sometimes differs from your Old Testament; the chapter notes point this out.

It is not a defence of slavery. Peter speaks to slaves in a world he could not change, and he calls their unjust treatment unjust. Using his words to defend slavery was a misuse, and it was wrong.

It is not a command to stay in danger. Nothing in its words to wives or slaves asks anyone to remain where they or their children are being harmed.

It is not a teaching that suffering is God's punishment. Peter speaks of suffering for doing good, and of a God who judges justly and will restore.

It is not contempt for the Jewish people. A Jewish apostle writes in Israel's own words to welcome Gentiles into Israel's blessings.

It is not a call to fight back, nor a call to hide. Peter's readers neither retaliate nor retreat. They do good, give a gentle answer, and trust God.

And it is not a map of the world after death. Its hardest verses are about Christ's victory, and these notes do not build more on them than they say.

Read it in one sitting, and read it as a real letter to frightened people.

Watch for its pattern: suffering, then glory, first for Christ and then for his people. Watch for the words that return: ‘hope’, ‘suffer’, ‘glory’, ‘grace’, ‘do good’, ‘exiles’. Notice how many of Israel's titles Peter gives to his readers, and ask what that meant to people who had lost their place in their towns.

Read the household passages slowly, and read them beside 2:21-25, the picture of Christ that they rest on. Read 3:18-22 with the whole letter in view, and do not let a puzzling verse hide its plain point.

Where churches differ, on election, on baptism, on marriage, on the spirits in prison, read more than one view before you settle, and hold your own view as one who may yet be taught.

And let it ask its questions. Where do you feel like a stranger? How do you answer people who speak against you? What is the reason for the hope that is in you?

The notes on each chapter go through it passage by passage in plain words.

hard.line: ‘Chosen according to the foreknowledge of God’: Reformed and Arminian readings, and the comfort they share.
Trials that test faith like gold: not punishment, and not to be faced alone.
Redeemed by ‘the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish’.
Israel's titles given to the church. The views on Israel, and the misuse rejected.
‘Honor the king’: respect for rulers, and fear for God alone.
Slaves and masters. Never a defence of slavery, and a misuse named.
Wives and husbands: the main readings, and nothing that asks anyone to stay in danger.
‘Always be prepared to give a defense’, with gentleness and respect.
The spirits in prison: three readings, no side.
‘Baptism that now saves you’: what all share, and where churches differ.
The gospel ‘preached even to those who are now dead’.
The fiery trial, and judgment that begins ‘with the family of God’.
‘Cast all your anxiety on Him’: an invitation, never a rebuke.

words.line: Greek parepidēmoi, people living away from home. God's people whose true home is elsewhere (1:1; 2:11).
Greek paroikoi, resident aliens without citizenship, as Abraham was among the Hittites (2:11; compare 1:17).
Greek anagennaō, to give new birth, found in the New Testament only in 1 Peter (1:3, 23).
Hope that rests on the resurrection of Jesus and looks to an inheritance that cannot spoil (1:3-4).
Greek lutroō, to set free by paying a price, as a slave or captive was freed (1:18-19).
Christ, rejected by people but chosen by God; believers too are living stones in his house (2:4-5).
Greek hierateuma, a body of priests. Peter gives Israel's title to the whole church (2:5, 9).
Greek hupogrammos, a model of letters a child traces when learning to write (2:21).
Greek apologia, a reasoned answer, as in a law court; the root of ‘apologetics’ (3:15).
Greek Christianos, a follower of Christ, one of only three uses in the New Testament (4:16).
Greek oikonomos, a household manager who handles what belongs to another (4:10).
Greek archipoimēn, found only here in the New Testament: Christ, to whom elders answer (5:4).

timeline.what: God waits patiently while the ark is built; eight people are saved through water (Genesis 6 to 8; 1 Peter 3:20).
Israel is redeemed from Egypt by the blood of the Passover lamb and called a kingdom of priests at Sinai (Exodus 12; 19:6).
Babylon destroys Jerusalem and carries Judah into exile.
Peter preaches in Jerusalem; among the hearers are people from Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia (Acts 2:9).
Silas, a leader in Jerusalem, is sent out with the council's letter and then travels with Paul (Acts 15:22, 40).
The great fire of Rome; Nero blames the Christians and has many put to death.
The letter is written from ‘Babylon’, most likely Rome, if Peter wrote it.
Early tradition says Peter died in Rome under Nero.
Rome destroys Jerusalem; Jewish writers begin to call Rome ‘Babylon’.
The date most often given by scholars who think the letter was written later in Peter's name.
Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia and Pontus, asks the emperor Trajan how to deal with Christians.
Irenaeus quotes the letter by name as Peter's.

places.name: Pontus
places.line: A province along the Black Sea coast. People from Pontus heard Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). How the gospel reached it is not known. Placed roughly.

places.name: Galatia
places.line: The inland province where Paul had founded churches (Acts 14; 16:6). Placed roughly.

places.name: Cappadocia
places.line: A province of the high inland plateau. People from Cappadocia heard Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). Placed roughly.

places.name: Asia
places.line: The Roman province of the west coast, with Ephesus its great city, where Paul had worked (Acts 19). Placed roughly.

places.name: Bithynia
places.line: A province on the coast south of the Black Sea. The Spirit kept Paul from entering it (Acts 16:7). Around AD 110 its governor, Pliny, wrote to the emperor about Christians there. Placed roughly.

places.name: Rome
places.line: Most readers take ‘Babylon’ (5:13) as a name for Rome, where early tradition places Peter at the end of his life. A few take it as Babylon in Mesopotamia or in Egypt.

teaching.mapNote: The letter went to believers in five provinces of Asia Minor (1:1). The names are placed roughly, as regions; their borders are not drawn. It was written from ‘Babylon’ (5:13), which most readers take to mean Rome. The letter does not say which towns its readers lived in.
